old_title: Trance, prog synths, guttural screaming: Lorenzo Senni's All Ages is the year's wildest electronic album
new_title: Is Lorenzo Senni's All Ages the year's wildest electronic album?
old_text:
The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni's Bandcamp page is striking. "Lorenzo Senni was never a raver," it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor's ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm's length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a "neon-hued chemical world".
A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini's hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled "rave voyeur" who "just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings". Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012's Quantum Jelly and 2014's Superimpositions featured what Senni called "pointillistic trance", spinning the icy, staccato notes and arpeggiated synth lines of the genre's epic breakdowns into lengthy, beatless tracks that never reached the climax implied. Released at the height of the 2020 Covid lockdown - when everyone was, by default, some distance from the dancefloor - his last album, Scacco Matto, expanded his palette to include lush ambient electronics, quasi-classical chord structures and something of the teeming chaos of Rustie's digital maximalism.
Six years on, All Ages approaches the tension of his initial encounters with dance music - the sober punk kid looking on intrigued - from a different angle. From its titular reference to booze-free punk gigs, to the straight-edge-symbolising Xs that litter the track names - Self eXamined Endurance, XGood Clean FunX - to the sound of skateboarder Jamie Thomas explaining how quitting drinking and weed "changed my life" on opener Art Life and Skateboarding, it makes Senni's own background more explicitly part of the action. Likewise the music, a bold, idiosyncratic attempt to meld what you might call Senni's trademark sound - a trebly, kick drum-free clutter of rave-y synth stabs, chattering trance-influenced electronics and more off-beam, occasionally atonal noises - with the hardcore punk that informed his teenage years. There are moments when the level of distortion applied to the electronics makes them vaguely resemble overdriven electric guitars. While there are tempo changes - the moment when Jealous of Michelangelo slows down momentarily gives the synth arpeggios a curiously proggy feel - there's a noticeable lack of dynamic shifts. It just blares at you, as indeed an old-fashioned loud-fast-rules hardcore band might.
Elsewhere, tracks are topped with vocal samples from Refused's Dennis Lyxzén, the late Tim Taylor of post-hardcore experimentalists Brainiac, and, in an impressive bit of crate-digging, Tom Loose, frontman of an obscure East Anglian metal band called Smokescreen. These are the most straightforward of Senni's attempts to square the circle between hard rock and avant-electronica, and the most successful. Raw throated and guttural, their voices are clearly the last thing you would expect to hear on top of music like this, but the effect isn't as jarring as you might think: on Self eXamined Endurance or Your Favourite DJ, they take on a propulsive, percussive quality, driving the tracks along in lieu of a beat. The results are exciting enough to counter any accusation that Senni is indulging in an arid, academic exercise. Likewise a collaboration with Xiu Xiu's Jamie Stewart, whose anguished voice pushes the warm, glitchy ambience of La Persuasione e la Rettorica into a new, more troubled emotional space.
Not everything here works as well as that. It's a big task that Senni has set himself, and it occasionally leads him to some curious places. You struggle to see what the lambent piano and strings of Purely Coincidental have to do with either punk or Senni's explorations of dance music: it just sounds like background music. Kill Lies All fits an emo-leaning vocal over chattering synths, which feels less like an expedition into hitherto uncharted musical territory and more like something a big name EDM producer would do (or rather has already done: Deadmau5 collaborated with My Chemical Romance frontman Gerard Way back in 2012).
Still, attempting to jam together two genres of music that have nothing in common beyond Senni's personal tastes is an intriguing task. If the hypothesis behind All Ages occasionally yields puzzling results, its failures aren't enough to warrant discounting the idea entirely. More often, the music doesn't really feel much like either of its sources, or indeed like anything else out there, and operates entirely according to its creator's strange internal logic: you feel like you're in the company of an original.
This week Alexis listened to
Fine - If You Wanna Come Down
Some tricky time signatures notwithstanding, Danish singer/songwriter Fine's second album Jazz Dreams certainly isn't jazz per se, but boasts an appealingly abstract, loose, wandering mood: If You Wanna Come Down is built for the small hours.
